title: The disappearance of the thylacine

paragraphs.text: Tasmania is the island state of Australia, and is located 240 kilometres south of the Australian mainland. One of the least understood of Tasmania's native animals is the thylacine. This animal, which is now thought to be extinct, looked like a large, long-bodied dog with a heavy, stiff tail. Its scientific name, Thylacinus cynocephalus, actually means a pouched dog with a wolf's head. However, because its body was covered with stripes, it was commonly known as the 'Tasmanian • tiger'. Thylacines, like many Australian animals, were marsupials, and had a pouch in which the young grew and travelled. As the young thylacines grew, their mothers' pouches expanded until they almost reached the ground. When they were old enough to leave the pouch, the young stayed in a lair such as a deep cave or hollow log while the mother hunted for food for them.

The thylacine was a meat-eater, which is unusual for a marsupial. They mainly hunted wallabies (animals similar to kangaroos), but they also hunted other small animals and birds. Most of the time thylacines were silent, but when they were hunting they gave a distinctive double yap, like a small dog, which they repeated every few seconds. They pursued their prey relentlessly, until the prey was exhausted. Thylacines were rarely seen to move fast, and when they did they appeared awkward, with a stiff trotting pace and an uncoordinated running stride. Despite its common name, 'tiger', the thylacine had a quiet, nervous temperament.

Thylacines once lived throughout Australia and New Guinea. Fossils and also Aboriginal rock paintings have been found that provide evidence of this. However, the most recent thylacine remains found outside Tasmania have been dated as being about 2,200 years old. Rivalry from dingoes (wild dogs) for prey and habitat may have contributed to the thylacine's disappearance from mainland Australia and New Guinea. Fortunately, the sea between mainland Australia and Tasmania protected the island population of thylacines from dingoes. Until the arrival of European settlers in 1803, thylacines had been widespread in Tasmania, but after only a century of European settlement the species was on the brink of extinction.

Unfortunately, thylacines began to prey upon settlers' sheep and chickens, and by 1830 there was a bounty on the thylacine. This meant that settlers got paid by the government for every thylacine they killed. As a result, records indicate that by the early 20th century there had been a significant decline in thylacine numbers. However, habitat destruction leading to population fragmentation is also believed to have been partly responsible for the decline in numbers. By the early decades of the 20th century there was recognition that thylacines were becoming rare, and zoos around the world became interested in obtaining them. The last known thylacine was captured in 1933 and kept in Hobart, the capital of Tasmania, where it died in 1936.

The thylacine was declared extinct in 1986 by international scientists. However, occasional sightings are still reported and so, although no proof has been provided for these sightings, some authorities are reluctant to make emphatic statements on the status of the species. But even if there are still a few remaining thylacines, it is unlikely that such a tiny population would have sufficient genetic diversity to allow for the viable continuation of the species. Recent attention has been given to the possibility of cloning. However, this is very unlikely to be achievable from the single remaining specimen thylacine that is preserved in alcohol. Even if cloning were possible, it should be asked whether such effort and expense are justifiable when many other species are currently threatened with extinction, and when the same processes that threaten habitats and wildlife are allowed to continue.

The thylacine is the only mammal to have been classed as extinct in Tasmania since European settlement. This is in vivid contrast to the situation on mainland Australia, which has the worst record of mammalian extinctions of any country on Earth, with nearly 50% of its native mammals having become extinct in the past 200 years. Tasmania is unique in that its fauna is abundant. It acts as a refuge for many species that have recently become extinct on mainland Australia. Perhaps the lesson to be learned from the loss of the.thylacine is to ensure that the rich natural heritage of Tasmania is not put at risk.
